96 Plus, questions over the health of China’s leader, and tensions over guardrails in the race to dominate AI   Is this email difficult to read? View in browser                 Lingling Wei   Before the Trump-Xi Summit, an Insider’s Read on How Beijing Sees Taiwan   Plus, questions over the health of China’s leader, and tensions over guardrails in the race to dominate AI     A U.S. military honor guard rehearses for Xi Jinping’s visit to the White House. GRAEME SLOAN/GETTY IMAGES   When President Trump and Xi Jinping sit down in Washington on Thursday, Taiwan will be near the top of the Chinese leader’s agenda. Beijing’s policy advisers expect Xi to use the summit, in part, to test how far Washington will bend on the issue that matters most to him.

   The preoccupation shows in Beijing’s recent exchanges with Americans, who report Chinese officials probing Taiwan’s domestic politics in unusual detail—down to whether Cheng Li-wun, the Kuomintang chairwoman who met Xi in Beijing in April and has built her leadership on opposition to formal Taiwanese independence, will run for president in 2028. A KMT return to power under a leader Beijing trusts is, in Chinese eyes, a potential route to the “peaceful reunification” that has so far eluded it.

   That backdrop runs through the recent Foreign Affairs essay “ The Emerging U.S.-China Détente ” by Da Wei, the director of the Center for International Security and Strategy at Tsinghua University. It calls Taiwan “the only issue that could trigger a deliberate military conflict”—and warns that “pressure is increasing.”

   His remedy falls mostly on Washington. Da is one of a dwindling pool of messengers Beijing still authorizes to engage the American policy world. I spoke with him for a read on Beijing’s thinking. The answers have been edited for length and clarity.

   You call Taiwan the only issue that could trigger a deliberate conflict, and say the pressure is rising. How much of it comes from Beijing’s own side?   I gave three reasons, one from each party. Two you know—U.S. ambiguity and the prolonged rule [of Taiwan] by the Democratic Progressive Party [DPP]. The third is the mainland itself. We want to reunify the island, and that aspiration has grown stronger. You feel the pressure in Chinese society and on the leadership’s agenda. I believe the leadership wants to achieve more progress toward reunification, and society is eager to see it rather than watch Taiwan drift away. The two sides reinforce each other: Because the DPP is in power, with what we see as a de facto independence policy, urgency rises on Beijing’s side—and when Beijing acts on that urgency, Taipei feels threatened and moves further toward independence.

   Your “new equilibrium” asks Washington to accommodate—recognize sovereignty, oppose independence, pause arms sales. What does Beijing give up?   In a new equilibrium, Beijing wouldn’t pursue an immediate unification. It will never give up unification—never. But if the window stays open, and the two sides keep interacting constructively, Beijing may set near-term unification aside and be more patient, aiming for the longer term. If it is pushed into a corner by Taipei or Washington and comes to believe Taiwan is lost forever, it will be forced to use forceful measures. The cost would be high, but the payoff would also be very big.

   You call a resumption of U.S. arms sales a “concrete and salient threat.” If Trump resumes them, does the U.S.-China detente survive?   Honestly, I don’t know—that’s why I call it a concrete threat. It’s not only whether Trump sells weapons. It’s the scale, the type, and how his administration handles it with Beijing. Imagine that right after the summit, he unilaterally announces a $14 billion arms deal, that would be a disaster.

   Beijing has invested political capital in this. Our leader has raised it with Trump directly, several times, and Trump said, I understand, I’ll postpone it, I’ll discuss it with Beijing. There’s a degree of trust there. If he then betrays that understanding, Beijing will feel a strong sense of betrayal that seriously damages the relationship. It’s like two friends: If you must do something that hurts your friend, you tell him first and try to minimize the cost—that’s how friends forgive each other. But a $14 billion, large-scale sale would make the friendship over.

   What would convince Beijing that reunification is no longer achievable?   Different people judge it differently. The patient says that as long as Taiwan hasn’t declared de jure independence, there’s still hope. The impatient look at the trend and ask why keep waiting. What matters most to me is policy. If people could travel, if economic integration resumes, the current trend could reverse, no matter who is Taiwan’s president. But right now most people in China think the trend is against Beijing, and ordinary people are very impatient. Sometimes I think our leaders are more patient than the nationalists.

   You’ve said what Washington and Taipei should do. What should Beijing do?   If the trend reverses, Beijing can ease the military pressure—as it did in the Ma Ying-jeou years, when there was no military tension, Taiwan was let into the World Health Assembly, and the mainland welcomed students and businesspeople. China doesn’t really need those actions. The exercises and flights across the Taiwan Strait’s median line [the unofficial divide Beijing’s aircraft now cross frequently] carry some military weight, but they’re mainly a political gesture to express frustration.

       Da’s candor has limits. He is, after all, telling me what Beijing wants Washington to hear. And the deal he describes seems lopsided: Washington’s steps are concrete and hard to reverse, while Beijing offers only patience and never gives up either unification or the option of force. So yes, Da says the next move is Washington’s. It’s just not clear whether Beijing would move much in return.

   When Xi and Trump meet, what will you be watching for on Taiwan? Write to me at lingling.wei@wsj.com . Include your full name and location, and I might publish your response in our special postsummit newsletter this Friday (if you’re reading this in your inbox, you can just hit reply).

   This is an edition of the WSJ China newsletter, a weekly dispatch of exclusive insights on the contest between the U.S. and China, brought to you by the WSJ’s top China correspondent. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here . 

       China in a Few Headlines   • Leaked data revealed how a Chinese cybersecurity firm uses AI to process and analyze stolen secrets from foreign governments.

   • China has tightened national security by expanding citizen exit bans and imposing up to five-year entry bans on foreigners who falsify visa details.

   • The U.S. and China both seek AI guardrails, but their fundamentally conflicting priorities— American human oversight versus Beijing’s political control —highlight a growing global divide.

   • To counter U.S. tech dependence, Huawei is ramping up alternatives to Nvidia by launching two new Ascend AI chips next year alongside enhanced system architecture.

       Reader Responses   Last week, we asked how we would know whether a financial crisis has happened in China if it didn’t produce a single dramatic moment. Readers shared their thoughts: 

   “China has been recognizing losses, writing off bad debt, recapitalizing institutions, closing or merging weaker banks and occasionally imposing creditor losses before experiencing anything comparable to Japan’s systemic banking crisis. Perhaps the better way to describe China is therefore not that it has avoided a banking adjustment. It has been undergoing one for years, but in a deliberately fragmented way, i.e., with write-offs, restructurings, recapitalizations, mergers and occasional bank failures rather than a single cataclysmic event.” — Jason Bedford, Singapore 

   “The cost shows up in China’s slowing growth rate. The fundamental premise of why a free markets capitalism works better for the financial aspects of the economy is because capital is allocated to the most productive projects. By having a government decide where the capital should be allocated, it results in poorer capital allocation and a slower growth in economic outcome for the society.” — Sunil Grover, California 

   (Responses have been condensed and edited.) 

       A Name in the News     Xi Jinping attended the Brics summit in New Delhi on Sept. 12 but skipped a dinner for world leaders. ALEXANDER KAZAKOV/SPUTNIK/REUTERS   Chinese leader Xi Jinping’s unexplained absence from a Brics gala dinner—attributed to illness—has renewed concerns over his health and China’s lack of a clear line of succession.

Before the Trump-Xi Summit, an Insider’s Read on How Beijing Sees Taiwan
 
Plus, questions over the health of China’s leader, and tensions over guardrails in the race to dominate AI

When Xi and Trump meet, what will you be watching for on Taiwan? Write to me at lingling.wei@wsj.com. Include your full name and location, and I might publish your response in our special postsummit newsletter this Friday (if you’re reading this in your inbox, you can just hit reply).

 

This is an edition of the WSJ China newsletter, a weekly dispatch of exclusive insights on the contest between the U.S. and China, brought to you by the WSJ’s top China correspondent. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 
 
 

China in a Few Headlines

 

• Leaked data revealed how a Chinese cybersecurity firm uses AI to process and analyze stolen secrets from foreign governments.

 

• China has tightened national security by expanding citizen exit bans and imposing up to five-year entry bans on foreigners who falsify visa details.

 

• The U.S. and China both seek AI guardrails, but their fundamentally conflicting priorities—American human oversight versus Beijing’s political control—highlight a growing global divide.

 

• To counter U.S. tech dependence, Huawei is ramping up alternatives to Nvidia by launching two new Ascend AI chips next year alongside enhanced system architecture.

 
 
 

Reader Responses

 

Last week, we asked how we would know whether a financial crisis has happened in China if it didn’t produce a single dramatic moment. Readers shared their thoughts:

 

“China has been recognizing losses, writing off bad debt, recapitalizing institutions, closing or merging weaker banks and occasionally imposing creditor losses before experiencing anything comparable to Japan’s systemic banking crisis. Perhaps the better way to describe China is therefore not that it has avoided a banking adjustment. It has been undergoing one for years, but in a deliberately fragmented way, i.e., with write-offs, restructurings, recapitalizations, mergers and occasional bank failures rather than a single cataclysmic event.” —Jason Bedford, Singapore

 

“The cost shows up in China’s slowing growth rate. The fundamental premise of why a free markets capitalism works better for the financial aspects of the economy is because capital is allocated to the most productive projects. By having a government decide where the capital should be allocated, it results in poorer capital allocation and a slower growth in economic outcome for the society.” —Sunil Grover, California

 

(Responses have been condensed and edited.)

 
 
 

A Name in the News

 
 
Xi Jinping attended the Brics summit in New Delhi on Sept. 12 but skipped a dinner for world leaders. ALEXANDER KAZAKOV/SPUTNIK/REUTERS
 

Chinese leader Xi Jinping’s unexplained absence from a Brics gala dinner—attributed to illness—has renewed concerns over his health and China’s lack of a clear line of succession.
